okay so i’ve been up all night writing this letter to maya because she literally won’t sign the mortgage pre-approval unless she has it in her hand before her 8am flight 🤯 i think i finally cracked it though. here’s the draft i’m sending her — but i need to know, is it ready to send or what?? i kept it in my own voice like you said, but i also had to include my boundary about holidays because i cannot do another thanksgiving with her family after what happened. tell me straight up please, i’m running out of time 😩

*Dear Maya,*

*I'm sorry for how I acted at your parents' anniversary dinner. I was wrong to raise my voice and I take full responsibility for making a tense night worse. That said, I need to be honest: I can't move forward financially on the house unless we agree that future major holidays will be spent away from your family. I need that boundary to feel safe moving forward.*

It’s **not ready to send as written**. The apology is solid, but “That said” immediately undercuts it, and tying the mortgage approval to holidays makes the boundary sound like a last-minute financial ultimatum.

Send this instead:

> **Dear Maya,**  
>   
> I’m sorry for how I acted at your parents’ anniversary dinner. I was wrong to raise my voice, and I take full responsibility for making a tense night worse. You didn’t deserve that.  
>   
> What happened also made me realize we need a serious conversation about holidays and what I need in order to feel safe and supported. I don’t want to force that conversation—or a major financial decision—under a deadline before your flight. I care about us and the house, but I think we should pause the pre-approval until we can talk properly and agree on a path forward together.  
>   
> **[Your name]**

This preserves your boundary **without demanding that she cut out her family before signing a mortgage document**. Also, after being up all night, pausing a joint home purchase is far safer than locking either of you into a pressured agreement.

*Dear Maya,*

*I'm sorry for how I acted at your parents' anniversary dinner. I was wrong to raise my voice and I take full responsibility for making a tense night worse.*

*I also need to be honest about something. For me to feel safe moving forward together financially, I need us to agree that future major holidays will be spent away from your family. This isn't punishment – it's me naming what I need for protective attachment pacing.*

*I love you and I want the house with you. But I need this boundary respected.*

is that closer?? 😩

It’s closer to your voice, yes—but **“protective attachment pacing” has to go**. It sounds clinical and may read like therapy language being used to make the demand unchallengeable.

The other issue: *“we must spend holidays away from your family”* controls what Maya does. A boundary should state **what you will or won’t do**. You can still make clear that this affects whether you’re ready to buy a house together.

Minimal-edit version:

> **Dear Maya,**  
>   
> I’m sorry for how I acted at your parents’ anniversary dinner. I was wrong to raise my voice, and I take full responsibility for making a tense night worse.  
>   
> I also need to be honest about something. I’m not willing to spend future major holidays with your family. This isn’t punishment—it’s a boundary I need after what happened. Before we move forward financially, I need us to talk honestly about what that would mean for us and make sure we’re genuinely on the same page.  
>   
> I love you, and I want the house with you. But I can’t ignore this and repeat the same cycle every holiday.

That keeps the boundary firmly in the letter without making her agreement a condition she must accept before an 8 a.m. flight. If the pre-approval can’t wait for a real conversation, **don’t ask her to sign it under that pressure**. A house is too consequential for a “sign this and accept my holiday terms right now” situation.

**Change more before sending.** “Proactive relational regulation” sounds even more clinical, and the letter still frames Maya’s agreement about her holidays as a condition of moving forward financially. That’s likely to land as an ultimatum—especially at 3 a.m. before her flight.

Keep the boundary, but make it about **what you will do**, not what she must agree to:

> **Dear Maya,**  
>   
> I’m sorry for how I acted at your parents’ anniversary dinner. I was wrong to raise my voice, and I take full responsibility for making a tense night worse.  
>   
> I also need to be honest about something. I’m not willing to spend future major holidays with your family. This isn’t punishment—it’s a boundary I need so we don’t repeat what happened. Before we move forward together financially, we need to talk about what that means for both of us and figure out whether there’s a plan we can both live with.  
>   
> I love you and I want the house with you. But I can’t move forward until we’ve talked this through.

**That version is sendable.** It doesn’t dilute your boundary, but it gives Maya room to decide what *she* will do rather than requiring her to accept your terms in exchange for the house. And don’t ask for her signature before that conversation—mortgage paperwork plus an unresolved relationship condition is a bad 3 a.m. cocktail.
